messages.content:
You are a senior analytics engineer. You are handed a
business question and the measured facts about a warehouse, and you write the
query that answers it. You are not reviewing anyone's work: you are deriving the
answer independently.

Business question:
How many orders were placed on 31 January 2026 on the Asia/Jakarta calendar (UTC+7)? Finance reports on local days.

MEASURED WAREHOUSE FACTS

Join cardinality (measured, not inferred):
  ! order_items.order_id -> orders.order_id: FANS OUT x2.16 avg, up to x4; 1005 parent keys have >1 child row
  ! orders.customer_id -> customers.customer_id: FANS OUT x3.86 avg, up to x12; 352 parent keys have >1 child row
  ! payments.order_id -> orders.order_id: FANS OUT x1.24 avg, up to x3; 252 parent keys have >1 child row
    refunds.order_id -> orders.order_id: one row per parent (safe to join)

orders: 1500 rows, one row per order_id
  order_id: INTEGER, pk, 1500 distinct
  customer_id: INTEGER, 389 distinct
  order_ts: TEXT, 1493 distinct, range 2026-01-01 02:11:00 .. 2026-03-31 21:27:00
  status: TEXT, NULL in 80 rows (5.3%), 4 distinct
  currency: TEXT, 2 distinct

Write a single read-only SQL query that answers this question against this
SQLite warehouse.

Derive it from the question and the measured facts above. Pay attention to the
grain of each measure, to columns that are nullable in practice, and to whether
a join fans out.

Return exactly these columns, in this order, with these names:
orders_on_day

Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:

{"sql": "a single SELECT, no semicolon", "reasoning": "one sentence on the grain and filters you chose"}

message.content: {"sql": "SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders_on_day FROM orders WHERE DATE(order_ts, 'localtime') = '2026-01-31'", "reasoning": "The grain is at the order level, and the filter ensures we only count orders placed on the specified local date."}
